case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a highly paid employee who is compensated on a daily-rate basis (without a guaranteed weekly salary) qualifies as an exempt “executive” under the FLSA, and thus is not entitled to overtime pay.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1) (the executive/administrative/professional exemptions), as implemented by the Department of Labor’s regulations—especially the ‘salary basis’ requirement in 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) and the special rule for daily-rate employees in 29 C.F.R. § 541.604(b).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Helix argues that Hewitt performed exempt executive duties and earned well above the regulatory salary threshold, so treating him as nonexempt solely because his compensation was calculated as a day rate elevates form over substance and conflicts with the purpose of the exemption for highly compensated executives; Helix contends the Fifth Circuit misread the regulations by requiring additional pay-structure guarantees (a weekly guarantee and a ‘reasonable relationship’ between the guarantee and actual pay) even for a very highly paid worker.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hewitt argues that the text of the DOL regulations makes ‘salary basis’ a separate, mandatory prerequisite to exemption: because Helix paid him only for days worked and did not guarantee a predetermined weekly amount regardless of hours/days worked, he was not paid on a salary basis; under 29 C.F.R. § 541.604(b), daily-rate pay can satisfy the salary-basis test only if the employer also provides a weekly guarantee and meets the regulation’s additional conditions—so he is entitled to overtime under the FLSA.
key_precedents: Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 138 S. Ct. 1134 (2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: Helix’s strongest “substance over form” argument—that Hewitt’s high day rate effectively guaranteed substantial weekly pay and should satisfy the executive exemption—runs headlong into the regulation’s structure: § 541.602(a) makes a predetermined weekly (or less frequent) amount a distinct prerequisite, and § 541.604(b) supplies the tailored route for day-rate pay only if there is a bona fide weekly guarantee plus a reasonable-relationship safeguard. Justice Barrett’s integrated reading of §§ 541.602 and 541.604(b) is particularly persuasive because it avoids rendering § 541.604(b) surplusage and yields an administrable, narrow rule grounded in text rather than purpose-driven revision. Justice Gorsuch’s Kisor point reinforces the institutional course here: we can decide on the regulation’s clear terms without invoking deference or creating an atextual carveout for highly compensated workers. Encino Motorcars’ “fair reading” principle does not authorize us to relax unambiguous regulatory conditions, and doing so would undermine predictable lines that preserve the legitimacy of the wage-and-hour regime.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Helix’s strongest argument is that Hewitt’s very high day rate and executive duties should make his compensation a “salary” in substance, but that invitation asks us to rewrite the Secretary’s duly promulgated definitions rather than apply their text. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, § 541.602(a)’s requirement of a predetermined amount paid on a weekly (or less frequent) basis and § 541.604(b)’s specific day-rate pathway—requiring a bona fide weekly guarantee and a reasonable-relationship condition—fit together, and Helix concedes it offered no such guarantee. Justice Gorsuch’s point about Kisor confirms we need not invoke any deference regime or purpose-driven gloss where ordinary tools show the regulation’s meaning is clear. Encino Motorcars’ “fair reading” principle does not authorize discarding unambiguous regulatory prerequisites that Congress expressly authorized the Secretary to “define and delimit.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Helix’s strongest point remains the practical-consequences/purpose argument: a highly paid supervisor looks like the kind of executive the exemption was meant to cover, and overtime here seems counterintuitive. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the regulatory scheme makes “salary basis” a separate, textually defined prerequisite, and § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined weekly (or less frequent) amount—something a pure day-rate does not provide. Justice Kavanaugh’s point is decisive on the text: § 541.604(b) is the specific route for day-rate compensation, and it demands a weekly guarantee plus a reasonable-relationship safeguard that Helix indisputably lacked; we cannot treat “high total pay” as a substitute for those conditions without rewriting the regulation. Encino Motorcars’ fair-reading principle supports applying the exemption as the regulation actually says, not loosening clear prerequisites in the name of purpose, and Kisor/Auer deference is unnecessary because the text resolves the issue.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Helix’s strongest point remains the “substance over form” argument that a very high day rate effectively guarantees substantial weekly compensation, but that functional gloss cannot displace the regulatory prerequisites that protect workers from schedule manipulation. As Justice Kagan stresses, the salary-basis rules supply an administrable, enforceable line; without an actual weekly guarantee, the worker bears the risk of fluctuations and the employer can evade overtime through day-allocation choices. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly read §§ 541.602(a) and 541.604(b) together: the latter is the specific, textually prescribed route for day-rate pay to count as salary and it requires both a weekly guarantee and a reasonable-relationship check—neither present here. Encino Motorcars’ “fair reading” does not authorize rewriting these clear conditions, and enforcing them advances fairness and access to justice by maintaining predictable protections even for highly paid workers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Helix’s strongest point remains the functional one: a very high day rate for an executive-level supervisor looks like the kind of compensation the exemption is meant to cover, so the salary-basis requirement can seem like empty formality. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively show that the regulatory scheme makes formality do real work—§ 541.602(a) sets a clear, administrable prerequisite (a predetermined weekly or less frequent amount), and § 541.604(b) is the tailored route for day-rate workers, demanding both a weekly guarantee and a reasonable-relationship check that Helix did not provide. Justice Gorsuch’s Kisor point reinforces my own methodology: because the text of the integrated regulations answers the question, we should not soften those express conditions based on perceived purpose or high total compensation. On a fair, coherent reading, § 541.601 does not silently waive salary basis; it incorporates it, and the absence of a weekly guarantee is dispositive.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest “substance over form” argument—that a very high day rate effectively assures weekly pay—cannot overcome the regulatory text requiring a “predetermined amount” paid “on a weekly, or less frequent basis,” § 541.602(a). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 541.604(b) is the tailored, specific pathway for day-rate arrangements to satisfy the salary-basis test, and it demands a bona fide weekly guarantee plus a reasonable-relationship condition—neither of which Helix provided—so treating high earnings as a substitute would render that provision largely superfluous. Justice Thomas’s point about Kisor reinforces my view that we need no deference: ordinary textual analysis resolves the meaning and leaves no warrant for an atextual carveout for highly compensated employees. Encino Motorcars’ “fair reading” supports enforcing clear regulatory prerequisites rather than rewriting them in the name of perceived statutory purpose.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is Helix’s functional argument that extraordinary day-rate pay plus executive duties should satisfy the highly compensated employee rule without the formal weekly guarantee, but the regulatory text makes “salary basis” an express prerequisite. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 541.601 incorporates the salary-basis requirement, § 541.602(a) defines it as a predetermined weekly (or less frequent) amount, and § 541.604(b) provides the specific, non-optional route for day-rate compensation—requiring a weekly guarantee and a reasonable-relationship check that Helix concedes it did not meet. Justice Gorsuch’s Kisor point reinforces that no deference or policy-driven gloss is needed; ordinary textual analysis of the integrated scheme resolves the case. Institutionally, adhering to these administrable, long-settled regulatory lines better preserves predictability and legitimacy than creating an atextual carveout for high earners.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest contention—that § 541.601’s highly compensated employee provision effectively relaxes the salary-basis requirement when total compensation is indisputably high—fails on the regulation’s text: § 541.601 expressly incorporates payment “on a salary basis,” and § 541.602(a) defines that term to require a predetermined amount paid weekly or less frequently. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 541.604(b) is not optional; it is the specific mechanism that allows day-rate pay to satisfy salary basis, but only with a bona fide weekly guarantee and a reasonable-relationship constraint—conditions Helix did not meet. Justice Gorsuch’s Kisor point reinforces that we do not need deference or purpose-driven “substance over form” reasoning to reach this result; ordinary interpretive tools show the weekly-guarantee requirement is a hard textual prerequisite. Encino Motorcars’ “fair reading” principle cannot justify rewriting these integrated regulatory conditions into an atextual exception for high earners.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best “spirit over form” argument—that Hewitt’s enormous day-rate earnings effectively guaranteed substantial weekly pay—fails because the regulations make an actual, predetermined weekly (or less frequent) amount a threshold condition, not a purpose-based proxy. As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, § 541.602(a) defines salary basis in administrable, procedural terms, and § 541.604(b) supplies the specific path for day-rate arrangements—requiring a bona fide weekly guarantee and a reasonable-relationship safeguard that Helix never provided. Encino Motorcars’ fair-reading approach, invoked by several colleagues, reinforces that we apply the regulatory text as written rather than create an atextual carveout for high earners that would invite manipulation of work schedules and undermine predictable overtime protections. No colleague offered a doctrinal basis to treat total annual compensation as a substitute for the regulatory weekly-guarantee prerequisite, so my vote remains with the Respondent.

John Roberts.reasoning: The governing regulations make “salary basis” a distinct prerequisite to the executive exemption, and § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined weekly amount not subject to reduction based on days worked; Helix’s day-rate scheme lacked that weekly guarantee. For employees paid on a daily basis, § 541.604(b) supplies the relevant path to satisfy the salary-basis test, and it expressly conditions exemption on a guaranteed weekly minimum and a “reasonable relationship” between the guarantee and actual earnings—requirements Helix did not meet. Respecting the Department of Labor’s long-standing reading of its own regulation (Auer v. Robbins) and adhering to the regulatory text avoids an atextual, purpose-driven expansion of exemptions and yields a narrow, administrable rule consistent with institutional legitimacy. Nothing in the FLSA, 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1), or the HCE framework in § 541.601 dispenses with the salary-basis requirement where, as here, there is no guaranteed weekly salary component.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 213(a)(1) exempts only those “employed in a bona fide executive…capacity,” and Congress expressly delegated to the Secretary authority to “define and delimit” that exemption; the valid, duly promulgated regulations therefore supply the operative, binding criteria for what qualifies as “executive.” Under the regulation’s text, “salary basis” requires a predetermined amount paid on a weekly (or less frequent) basis, 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a), and daily-rate arrangements satisfy that test only if the employer also provides a weekly guarantee meeting the additional conditions in § 541.604(b)—which Helix did not. While I have serious doubts about deference regimes that let agencies expand their own power, this case can be resolved by the regulations’ plain text without resort to Auer, and nothing in the statute’s original meaning compels ignoring those regulatory prerequisites. Accordingly, Hewitt was not paid on a “salary basis” as the regulation requires and is entitled to overtime.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The DOL’s regulations implementing 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1) make payment on a “salary basis” a distinct prerequisite to the executive exemption, and § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined weekly amount not subject to reduction based on the quantity of work performed. Where, as here, compensation is computed on a day-rate with no weekly guarantee, the special rule in § 541.604(b) supplies the only path for treating day-rate pay as a “salary,” and it expressly demands both a minimum weekly guarantee and a “reasonable relationship” between that guarantee and actual earnings. Helix’s “substance over form” argument cannot overcome the regulation’s text, and under Encino Motorcars the Court gives FLSA exemptions a fair reading without rewriting clear regulatory conditions; Auer likewise underscores that the salary-basis requirement turns on the regulatory terms, not general appeals to purpose.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Department of Labor’s regulations make “salary basis” an independent prerequisite to the executive exemption, requiring a predetermined amount paid on a weekly (or less frequent) basis that is not reduced based on the quantity of work. 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a). When an employer pays a day rate, the regulations provide a specific path to satisfy salary basis only if there is a guaranteed weekly amount and the guarantee bears a “reasonable relationship” to the amount actually earned. 29 C.F.R. § 541.604(b). Even after Encino Motorcars rejected a narrow-construction canon for FLSA exemptions, it still demands a fair reading of the governing text; here the regulatory text is clear that high total compensation alone cannot substitute for the missing weekly guarantee, and denying overtime in this pay structure would erode predictable, enforceable protections for workers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FLSA’s executive exemption, as implemented by the Department of Labor, makes the “salary basis” requirement a distinct prerequisite: § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined amount paid on a weekly (or less frequent) basis that is not subject to reduction based on the quantity of work. For employees paid on a daily rate, § 541.604(b) provides the path to satisfy the salary-basis test—but only if there is a weekly guarantee at least equal to the minimum required amount and a “reasonable relationship” between that guarantee and actual earnings; Helix’s pay scheme lacks those features. While petitioner’s policy arguments about highly compensated executives have some force, the regulatory text supplies a workable, administrable line that preserves statutory coherence and prevents employers from evading overtime through nominal guarantees. Under Auer v. Robbins, the salary-basis framework is a core component of the exemption regulations, and nothing in § 541.601’s high-compensation provision eliminates the baseline requirement that compensation be on a salary basis as defined in § 541.602 and, for day-rate workers, § 541.604(b).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The governing regulations make “salary basis” a distinct prerequisite to the FLSA’s executive exemption, and § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined amount paid on a weekly (or less frequent) basis that is not reduced because of variations in work performed. A daily-rate arrangement, standing alone, does not satisfy that plain textual requirement; § 541.604(b) confirms that day-rate pay may qualify only if accompanied by a guaranteed weekly amount and other conditions. Under Kisor v. Wilkie, there is no occasion to defer to any agency gloss where the regulatory text supplies the answer using ordinary tools of interpretation, and any remaining doubt in an overtime-setting counsels against expanding the exemption beyond its terms. Accordingly, an employee paid solely by the day without a weekly guarantee is not exempt and is entitled to overtime.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The governing regulations make the “salary basis” requirement a distinct prerequisite to the executive exemption: § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined amount paid on a weekly (or less frequent) basis, and § 541.604(b) provides the specific path for daily-rate pay—requiring a weekly guarantee and a “reasonable relationship” between the guarantee and actual earnings. Helix paid Hewitt purely by the day with no guaranteed weekly amount, so under the regulatory text he was not paid on a salary basis and therefore does not qualify for the exemption in 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1) as implemented by the DOL. Respect for settled regulatory structure and administrable rules favors applying § 541.604(b) as written rather than creating an exception for highly paid workers based on purpose or equitable considerations. Encino Motorcars confirms we apply exemptions by their text and ordinary tools of interpretation, not by artificially narrowing or broadening them, and here the text of the salary-basis rules forecloses Helix’s position.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The operative regulatory text makes "salary basis" an independent prerequisite to the § 213(a)(1) exemptions, requiring a "predetermined amount" paid "on a weekly, or less frequent basis" that is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quantity of work. 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a). For employees whose earnings are computed on an hourly, daily, or shift basis, § 541.604(b) supplies the specific mechanism to satisfy the salary-basis requirement—demanding a weekly guarantee meeting the minimum and a "reasonable relationship" between the guarantee and actual earnings—which Helix did not provide. Reading §§ 541.602(a) and 541.604(b) together, and giving effect to each, the absence of a weekly guarantee forecloses exemption even for a highly paid worker, and Encino Motorcars does not authorize rewriting the regulations to avoid that textual condition.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FLSA’s exemptions apply only if the employer satisfies the Department of Labor’s regulatory prerequisites, including the “salary basis” requirement in 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a), which demands a predetermined weekly amount not subject to reduction based on the quantity of work performed. Where, as here, compensation is computed solely on a daily-rate basis, the regulations supply a specific pathway—29 C.F.R. § 541.604(b)—that requires a weekly guarantee and a “reasonable relationship” between that guarantee and actual earnings; Helix did not provide that guarantee, so the exemption is not met. This reading honors procedural fairness by applying the rule as written and avoids eroding overtime protections through pay-structure labels, even for highly compensated workers, consistent with the Court’s insistence that exemptions turn on the regulatory text rather than employer characterizations. Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro supports focusing on the statutory and regulatory language rather than policy-driven “purpose” arguments to expand an exemption beyond its terms.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a highly paid employee who is paid only a daily rate (with no guaranteed weekly pay) can qualify as an FLSA “bona fide executive” exempt from overtime under the Department of Labor’s “salary basis” regulation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1) (executive/administrative/professional exemptions), implemented via U.S. Department of Labor regulations defining payment on a “salary basis,” chiefly 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) and the special rule for daily-rate workers, 29 C.F.R. § 541.604(b) (and related “highly compensated employee” regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 541.601).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Helix argues Hewitt was exempt because he performed executive duties and earned very high compensation; it contends that paying a day-rate that always resulted in weekly earnings well above the regulatory minimum should satisfy (or effectively satisfy) the salary-basis requirement, and that the Fifth Circuit’s contrary reading of the regulations is overly formalistic, conflicts with how the exemption framework is supposed to operate for highly compensated executives, and would disrupt longstanding pay practices in offshore/oil-and-gas operations.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hewitt argues he was non-exempt because Helix paid him on a pure day-rate with no guaranteed weekly amount regardless of hours/days worked, which fails the plain text of the DOL’s salary-basis test; under the regulations (especially § 541.602(a) and § 541.604(b)), a daily-rate worker is exempt only if the employer also provides a guaranteed weekly amount meeting the minimum and meeting the ‘reasonable relationship’ requirement—something Helix did not do—so he is entitled to overtime notwithstanding his high total earnings.
key_precedents: Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt, 598 U.S. 39 (2023)
Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 584 U.S. 79 (2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s ultra vires point—§ 213(a)(1) speaks in duties terms and does not itself mention a salary basis—poses the strongest challenge, but this case is most properly decided on the clear, controlling regulatory text the parties litigated under, not by reaching out to invalidate the regulation on an undeveloped theory. As Justice Kagan stresses, § 541.601(b) expressly incorporates § 541.602’s salary-basis requirement, and §§ 541.602(a) and 541.604(b) draw a bright line: day-rate pay can qualify only with a guaranteed weekly minimum and a reasonable relationship, which Helix concededly lacked. Justice Barrett’s invocation of Encino Motorcars reinforces that we apply exemptions (and their implementing regulations) as written without a thumb on the scale, but it does not license disregarding an unambiguous weekly-guarantee condition. Given Helix Energy Solutions v. Hewitt’s recent application of this same framework, minimalism and institutional legitimacy counsel a narrow holding enforcing the regulation as written and leaving any broader statutory-delegation challenge for a case that squarely presents it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that, as a matter of regulatory text, §§ 541.602(a) and 541.604(b) plainly require a guaranteed weekly minimum and Helix did not provide one. But that only moves the question back a step: Congress in § 213(a)(1) exempted “bona fide executive” employees based on role and duties, and I do not read the “define and delimit” delegation—invoked by Justice Alito and Justice Sotomayor—as authority to add a freestanding salary-basis bookkeeping prerequisite that excludes an undisputed executive solely because compensation is computed per day. Helix Energy Solutions v. Hewitt shows the Court has recently applied the regulation as written, yet it does not resolve whether the regulation is consistent with the statute’s original public meaning or within the agency’s delegated power, and I would not treat longevity or administrability as a substitute for legality. Encino Motorcars, which Justice Barrett cites, reinforces that we apply texts as written without a thumb on the scale; here, that principle cuts against letting an atextual regulatory condition contract the exemption beyond what Congress enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press that § 213(a)(1) speaks in terms of duties and does not itself mention “salary basis,” but that point does not carry the day given Congress’s express delegation to the Department of Labor to “define and delimit” the exemption and the clarity of the regulatory conditions the agency adopted. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, our task in this case is to apply the governing regulatory text, not to craft an industry-specific carveout or revisit the wisdom of the agency’s line-drawing in the abstract; Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt underscores that these very provisions—§§ 541.602(a) and 541.604(b)—are to be enforced as written. Justice Kagan’s observation that § 541.601(b) expressly incorporates the salary-basis requirement “pursuant to § 541.602” is dispositive against the idea that high total pay can substitute for the missing weekly guarantee. Even under a practical-consequences lens, accepting petitioner’s approach would invite easy evasion by re-labeling weekly salaries as day rates, undermining the administrable notice function the regulation supplies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that § 213(a)(1) itself does not mention a salary basis and thus the exemption should turn only on duties—does not persuade me because Congress delegated to the Department of Labor the task of defining and delimiting the exemption, and the agency reasonably chose salary-basis safeguards to prevent overtime evasion through variable pay schemes. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the regulatory text is clear: § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined weekly amount not reduced based on days worked, and § 541.604(b) is the specific, exclusive route for day-rate arrangements, requiring a weekly guarantee plus a “reasonable relationship” to actual earnings—terms Helix concededly did not meet. Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt confirms that even the highly compensated employee rule incorporates, rather than displaces, these salary-basis prerequisites, which protect workers’ predictable access to overtime remedies in grueling, high-hours settings. Whatever one thinks of the policy tradeoffs, I cannot rewrite the regulation to treat high total pay as a substitute for the weekly-guarantee requirement the agency adopted to secure administrable fairness.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that § 213(a)(1) does not itself mention “salary basis” and focuses on duties—raises an important ultra vires question in the abstract, but it does not destabilize our disposition in this case as litigated. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Helix did not squarely preserve a regulation-invalidity theory, and the operative regulatory text is clear: § 541.601(b) expressly requires payment on a salary-basis “pursuant to § 541.602,” while § 541.604(b) provides the only way a day-rate can satisfy that requirement (a guaranteed weekly minimum plus a reasonable relationship), which Helix concededly lacked. Encino Motorcars, noted by Justice Barrett, reinforces that we apply exemptions and their regulatory definitions as written without skewing presumptions—but it does not authorize us to rewrite the regulation to treat high total compensation as a substitute for the weekly-guarantee condition the regulation adopts. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, the most coherent and administrable course is to apply the duly promulgated regulatory scheme as written and leave any recalibration to the agency.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious objection: § 213(a)(1) speaks in terms of “bona fide executive” duties and does not itself mention a salary-basis prerequisite, so one might question whether the Department may add that requirement. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, this case is litigated within a duly promulgated regulatory scheme whose text is unambiguous: § 541.602(a) demands a predetermined weekly (or less frequent) amount not varying with work performed, and § 541.604(b) provides the exclusive mechanism for day-rate pay to qualify—via a guaranteed weekly minimum plus a reasonable-relationship safeguard—neither of which Helix supplied. Encino Motorcars, noted by Justice Barrett, reinforces that we apply exemptions as written without extra “narrow construction” gloss, yet it likewise does not license us to disregard clear regulatory prerequisites or to create an atextual carveout. If the regulation is ultra vires, that challenge should be squarely presented; absent that, separation-of-powers principles counsel applying the regulatory text as written rather than revising it in adjudication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that § 213(a)(1) does not itself mention a salary basis and thus the regulation allegedly narrows the statute—raises a serious ultra vires question, but it does not undermine disposition in this vehicle given Congress’s express delegation to the Department to “define and delimit” the exemption and the Court’s longstanding acceptance of salary-basis line-drawing as administrable within that delegation. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, we can (and should) resolve the case on the clear regulatory text Helix chose to litigate under: §§ 541.602(a) and 541.604(b) require a guaranteed weekly minimum (and, for day rates, a reasonable relationship), which Helix did not provide. Justice Kagan’s point is decisive for Helix’s HCE fallback: § 541.601(b) expressly incorporates the salary-basis requirement “pursuant to § 541.602,” so high annual pay cannot substitute for the missing weekly guarantee. Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt is directly on point and, as an institutional matter, I see no principled way to carve out an atextual exception here without inviting regulated parties to bypass unambiguous prerequisites.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is antecedent and statutory: § 213(a)(1) speaks in terms of “bona fide executive” duties and does not itself mention a salary basis, so he argues the Department exceeded its authority by adding that prerequisite. But the statute’s text delegates to the Department the power to “define and delimit” the exemption, and (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress) the governing regulations unambiguously make a salary-basis showing mandatory even under the highly compensated pathway because § 541.601(b) incorporates § 541.602. On the regulatory text, a pure day-rate necessarily varies with days worked and thus cannot satisfy § 541.602(a)’s “predetermined amount … not subject to reduction,” while § 541.604(b) supplies the exclusive mechanism for daily-rate pay to qualify—requiring a guaranteed weekly minimum Helix did not provide. Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt confirms that our role here is to apply those clear regulatory conditions as written, not to create an atextual exception for highly paid day-rate executives or to entertain an underdeveloped ultra vires challenge in this vehicle.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that § 213(a)(1) mentions only “bona fide executive” duties and not a salary-basis requirement—does not overcome that Congress expressly delegated to the Department of Labor the task of “defin[ing] and delimit[ing]” the exemption, and the agency’s regulatory line-drawing is textually clear and administrable. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 541.602(a) demands a predetermined amount not subject to reduction with the quantity of work, and § 541.604(b) specifically addresses day-rate pay by allowing exemption only with a guaranteed weekly minimum and a reasonable-relationship constraint—protections Helix did not provide. Even accepting the policy intuition that very high daily pay “looks like” exempt compensation, the practical consequence of abandoning the weekly-guarantee rule would be to invite evasive pay structuring and reduce fair notice about overtime eligibility for workers who experience large hour swings. Encino Motorcars does not justify rewriting these regulations; it counsels applying the relevant texts neutrally rather than expanding exemptions beyond the conditions the agency adopted.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of the Department of Labor’s salary-basis regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a), requires a predetermined amount paid on a weekly (or less frequent) basis not subject to reduction based on the quantity of work, and § 541.604(b) provides the exclusive path for exempting day-rate workers—requiring a guaranteed weekly amount plus a “reasonable relationship” to actual earnings. Helix paid Hewitt a pure daily rate with no weekly guarantee, so he does not satisfy the salary-basis test even if his total compensation was high, and the highly compensated employee rule in § 541.601 still incorporates the salary-basis requirement “pursuant to § 541.602.” A narrow, regulation-text-based disposition best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy by applying the DOL’s chosen framework rather than rewriting it to accommodate particular industry pay practices. Consistent with Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt, the exemption cannot be expanded beyond the regulatory conditions Congress authorized the agency to implement under 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 213(a)(1) exempts from overtime any employee employed in a "bona fide executive" capacity, and its text contains no "salary basis" requirement; the exemption turns on duties, not the pay’s bookkeeping form. To the extent 29 C.F.R. §§ 541.602(a), 541.604(b), and 541.601 categorically deny exempt status to an undisputed executive solely because he is paid a day rate without a guaranteed weekly minimum, those regulations narrow the statutory exemption beyond the FLSA’s original public meaning and exceed the Department’s implementing authority. I would therefore reject the respondent’s reliance on the regulatory gloss and apply the statute’s text, which Helix satisfies on the conceded executive-duties facts. Where precedent suggests deference to agency interpretations of such regulations (Auer v. Robbins), I would not extend it to uphold a regulation that conflicts with the statute’s text and structure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Department of Labor’s regulations make the “salary basis” a condition of the § 213(a)(1) exemption, and § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined weekly (or less frequent) amount paid regardless of days or hours worked—something a pure day-rate arrangement does not provide. Section 541.604(b) supplies the specific path for daily-rate workers to satisfy the salary-basis concept, but only if there is a guaranteed weekly amount meeting the minimum and a “reasonable relationship” to actual earnings; Helix concededly offered no such guarantee. The highly compensated employee rule in § 541.601 still incorporates the salary-basis requirement (via § 541.602), so high total pay cannot substitute for the text’s guaranteed-weekly-pay condition. This reading follows Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt, 598 U.S. 39 (2023), which applied the regulatory text as written rather than rewriting it based on policy objections or industry practice.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FLSA’s overtime protections are the rule, and exemptions under 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1) must be applied as the Department of Labor’s regulations require, not stretched based on an employee’s high total pay. Under 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a), a worker is paid on a “salary basis” only if he receives a predetermined weekly amount not subject to reduction based on days worked; and for day-rate arrangements, § 541.604(b) allows exemption only when the employer also guarantees a weekly amount meeting the minimum and bears a “reasonable relationship” to actual weekly earnings—conditions Helix did not satisfy. Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt (2023) confirms that even “highly compensated” status under § 541.601 does not displace § 541.604(b)’s safeguards, which prevent employers from evading overtime by labeling variable, day-based compensation as a salary. Enforcing the regulation’s clear prerequisites fairly protects workers who routinely work extreme hours (often on remote rigs) and preserves predictable access to overtime remedies.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The regulations make salary-basis status a prerequisite even for the highly compensated employee pathway: § 541.601(b) requires at least the weekly minimum to be paid “on a salary … basis” as defined in § 541.602, and a pure day-rate with no guaranteed weekly amount does not satisfy § 541.602(a)’s requirement of a predetermined amount not subject to reduction based on days worked. For employees paid on a daily (or hourly/shift) basis, § 541.604(b) supplies the only route to treat that pay as “salary basis,” and it demands both a guaranteed weekly amount meeting the minimum and a “reasonable relationship” to actual earnings—conditions Helix did not meet. That textual structure yields a workable, coherent rule: high total pay alone cannot substitute for the specific weekly guarantee the agency required, consistent with Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt (2023).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The governing text is the Department’s salary-basis rule: § 541.602(a) requires a predetermined amount paid on a weekly (or less frequent) basis, and § 541.604(b) permits day-rate compensation only if the employer also guarantees a weekly amount meeting the minimum and ensures a “reasonable relationship” between that guarantee and actual earnings—conditions Helix did not satisfy. Whatever the policy appeal of treating very high daily-rate earnings as “close enough,” courts must apply the regulation’s plain terms rather than revise them in light of perceived industry practice, consistent with separation-of-powers principles and skepticism of administrative rewriting through litigation. Nor does the highly compensated employee provision, § 541.601, dispense with the salary-basis requirement; it expressly ties the required weekly payment to § 541.602, so a pure day-rate lacking a guaranteed weekly amount cannot qualify. This reading accords with Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt, 598 U.S. 39 (2023), and avoids expanding exemptions beyond their enacted and promulgated limits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the text of the Department of Labor’s regulations, the “salary basis” rule requires a predetermined amount paid each pay period that is “not subject to reduction because of variations in the … quantity of the work performed,” and the employee must receive the full salary for any week in which he performs any work, “without regard to the number of days or hours worked.” 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a). A pure day-rate arrangement, with no guaranteed weekly amount, makes weekly pay turn on days worked and therefore does not satisfy § 541.602(a); where pay is computed on a daily basis, § 541.604(b) provides the path to exemption only if there is a guaranteed weekly minimum meeting the regulatory threshold and a “reasonable relationship” between the guarantee and actual earnings—requirements Helix did not meet. Precedent and practical workability favor applying the regulations as written rather than creating an atextual carveout based on high annual compensation, especially because the HCE rule itself requires at least the weekly minimum be paid on a salary basis. See 29 C.F.R. § 541.601(b); Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt, 598 U.S. 39 (2023).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of the Department of Labor’s salary-basis regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a), requires a predetermined amount paid each pay period “not subject to reduction” because of variations in work performed, which a pure day-rate arrangement does not provide. Where pay is computed on a daily basis, § 541.604(b) supplies the conditions for maintaining exempt status—most notably a guaranteed weekly amount paid regardless of days worked and a “reasonable relationship” between that guarantee and actual earnings—and Helix concedes it provided no such guarantee. The highly compensated employee provision, § 541.601, still incorporates the salary-basis requirement via § 541.602(a), so high total earnings cannot substitute for the regulation’s textual guarantee. This reading follows Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt, 598 U.S. 39 (2023), and is consistent with Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 584 U.S. 79 (2018), in applying the exemption as written rather than expanding it beyond the regulatory text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Department of Labor’s salary-basis rule requires a worker to receive, each pay period, a predetermined amount “not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of the work performed,” 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a); a pure day-rate with no guaranteed weekly minimum does not satisfy that text. The special daily-rate provision, 29 C.F.R. § 541.604(b), confirms that when pay is computed on a daily basis the exemption is available only if the employer also provides a guaranteed weekly amount meeting the minimum salary level and maintaining a “reasonable relationship” to actual earnings—protections Helix did not provide, regardless of Hewitt’s high total pay. As the Court held in Helix Energy Solutions Group, Inc. v. Hewitt, the regulatory scheme draws a deliberate line that promotes administrable, fair notice to workers about overtime eligibility and prevents evasion through nominally “high” but variable compensation. Encino Motorcars does not permit rewriting the regulations’ clear requirements; the exemption turns on the regulatory salary-basis conditions, not simply on job title and large annual earnings.
